It’s been a few months now testing the @maticrobots vacuum cleaner

Before we had a Roborock (essentially a Roomba knockoff)

But the Roborock became kinda useless, it'd always get stuck in any type of cable, it'd always get stuck not being able to get on to the thick rug, so you'd have to prep the room every single time just to use it

Too much work so we just stopped using it

The Matic is, well, completely different. It's not flat or low, it's a chunky tall kinda cute looking cube shaped thing with 2 big wheels

And it's a different philosophy, it has cameras and tries to understand its environment, more like a modern robot or a self driving Tesla than a classic Roomba-type vacuum

That makes it just way way better, it doesn't get stuck in cables, it doesn't get stuck in rugs, it drives and turns around the room almost like a mini car

It's also way more silent than Roborock or Roomba-type vacuums, and measurably way more powerful in both vacuuming and mopping

They also respond very fast to feedback and improve things fast, like companies should be these days (instead of getting stuck in some hellish corporate support flow)

Another thing, I don't trust consumer devices connected to the internet (and nor should you) so of course I asked to Claude to analyze if it was phoning home (remember the other vacuums who upload your house plan to China, that was true). Claude was conclusive, Matic never phoned home anything, excellent

Maybe the best part is, it just looks cute and you wanna anthropomorphize it, and they include 2 googly eye stickers so it becomes even more like a dog/cat/pet

@mehul made a great thing!

1. Start with ONE agent

One model. One context window. One loop.

Load skills + tools only when needed.

Don't build a multi-agent system before you've proven you need one.

2. Keep subagents only when they earn their place

Three good reasons:

• Context bloat measurably hurts performance
• Tasks can run in parallel with fresh, disposable context
• One agent struggles to select tools or handle conflicting instructions

Otherwise, simplify.

3. Every handoff loses context

Multiple agents passing summaries back and forth create a game of telephone.

Details get lost. Latency adds up.

One customer saw ~2x faster runtime after moving to a single-agent loop.

4. Bloated prompt? Use skills, not more agents

Stop stuffing every instruction into one giant system prompt.

Load domain knowledge only when needed.

Anthropic says it cut Claude Code's system prompt by over 80% for newer models, partly through this approach.

5. Watch your tool count

Anthropic found that tool selection tends to degrade beyond 30–50 tool definitions in the system prompt.

Group tools by user intent.

Use on-demand tool loading instead of exposing everything at once.

6. Fold ONE subagent at a time

The migration process:

• Turn prompts into skills
• Turn API calls into MCP tools
• Run evals before + after
• Keep only changes that improve results

Just 10 golden examples are enough to start evaluating.

7. Don't trust the overall score
Check which specific tasks improved or broke.
In Anthropic's own test, folding a subagent reduced latency but broke a previously working process.
Run each task multiple times.

The takeaway:

Your AI agent shouldn't be a copy of your org chart.

Start simple. Measure everything. Add complexity only when it earns its place.

▲ Nace AI just released Drex for Search, which brings its Drex decision models to document search, so AI agents get cited pages instead of top-k chunks.

The key idea is that search is a series of decisions. Drex first classifies the question as a quick lookup or a deeper agent search. It then narrows the workspace from folder to file, section and page, down to table and column inside a sheet. Only the kept pages reach the LLM, and the answer cites the file and page.

On OfficeQA Pro, all 9 agent setups Nace tested needed fewer turns, with Claude Code on Opus 5.5 going from 18.5 to 9.1 turns.

Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode can call it through the nace-mcp server or the CLI. There are also Python and TypeScript SDKs and a REST API......

I kept closing my MacBook while Claude Code was still working. Every time, the work just stopped. macOS sleeps the second the lid closes, and the keep-awake apps I tried only stop idle sleep.

So I made Double Shot ☕

A tiny menu bar app that keeps your Mac awake while your AI agents work, even with the lid closed.

It knows when Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI or Cursor are actually working, not just open. Background runs like claude -p count until they're done. When everything goes quiet, your Mac sleeps like normal again.

It also looks after the Mac in your bag. It turns the screen off, switches on Low Power Mode, stops if it gets warm, and puts the Mac to sleep when the work is done.

You can still use it the simple way too: keep the Mac awake for 30 minutes, or until you turn it off. The panel is a little espresso glass, you pour time in and watch it drain.

Free and open source:
https://t.co/TPWKm8D1BI

Or with Homebrew:
brew install --cask noahelhadedy/tap/double-shot

virals.text:
"Hey, let's attack the castle!" (voice command while riding a dragon). Ok, you got me there. If that kind of simulation is possible, I want to try it.

Genie 4 is out, Google's first world model for real-time interactive simulation.

I've been following world models for a while. Below are a few interesting points for folks not familiar with world models.

What are world models?
🧠 AI that learns to predict what happens next, then uses that to plan and learn
🔮 LLMs predict the next word, world models predict what happens next in the world
🏗️ Main approaches: JEPA (LeCun), Genie 4 (DeepMind), Marble (World Labs), Cosmos (NVIDIA)
🆕 Genie 4 (announced today) simulates interactive 3D worlds frame by frame, in real time, with native audio

Use cases of world models:
🤖 Robotics: plan motions, train on imagined trajectories (DeepMind paired Genie 4 with Gemini in robotics research)
🚗 Driving: Waymo built its World Model on Genie 3 to simulate edge cases
🎮 Games and VR: steer live worlds with text, like changing weather or adding characters
🎬 Creative industries: filmmaking, journalism, gaming, manufacturing
📊 Enterprise “what-if” simulation before acting

Advantages of world models:
💰 Cheaper and safer than physical testing
📉 Synthetic data where real data is slow and expensive
🧩 Better causal reasoning and long-horizon planning than LLMs
🔊 Richer simulations: Genie 4 adds audio, dialogue and more realistic physics
🤝 Pairs with LLMs: Genie 4 uses Gemini models to keep scenes coherent

Some caveats:
⏱️ Genie 4 stays consistent for only about two minutes, and details drift over longer runs
🔒 Genie 4 is research preview only, for trusted testers
📏 A May 2026 benchmark found no model above 52% on physical consistency
🔥 Resource-hungry, and they can still hallucinate

Future of world models:
💸 Over $3B in VC went to world-model startups in H1 2026
🚀 DeepMind calls world simulation a crucial step toward AGI
🔀 Likely a hybrid future: LLMs, agents and world models combined
🧪 Wider Genie 4 access is coming soon via Project Genie and the Gemini API
🎯 Evaluation needs to go beyond visual realism

▲ Nace AI just released Drex for Search, which brings its Drex decision models to document search, so AI agents get cited pages instead of top-k chunks.

The key idea is that search is a series of decisions. Drex first classifies the question as a quick lookup or a deeper agent search. It then narrows the workspace from folder to file, section and page, down to table and column inside a sheet. Only the kept pages reach the LLM, and the answer cites the file and page.

The numbers, per Nace: 92.05% on BrowseComp-Plus with GPT-5, at 12.61 search calls per question, 16.6x fewer than the only entry ahead. 77.5% R@1 on VisDocAgentBench, 10 points above Claude Opus 5. 94.7% on MADQA with Gemini 3.5 Flash. On OfficeQA Pro, all 9 agent setups Nace tested needed fewer turns, with Claude Code on Opus 5.5 going from 18.5 to 9.1 turns.

Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode can call it through the nace-mcp server or the CLI. There are also Python and TypeScript SDKs and a REST API......

I kept closing my MacBook while Claude Code was still working. Every time, the work just stopped. macOS sleeps the second the lid closes, and the keep-awake apps I tried only stop idle sleep.

So I made Double Shot ☕

A tiny menu bar app that keeps your Mac awake while your AI agents work, even with the lid closed.

It knows when Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI or Cursor are actually working, not just open. Background runs like claude -p count until they're done. When everything goes quiet, your Mac sleeps like normal again.

It also looks after the Mac in your bag. It turns the screen off, switches on Low Power Mode, stops if it gets warm, and puts the Mac to sleep when the work is done.

You can still use it the simple way too: keep the Mac awake for 30 minutes, or until you turn it off. The panel is a little espresso glass, you pour time in and watch it drain.

Free and open source:
https://t.co/TPWKm8D1BI

Or with Homebrew:
brew install --cask noahelhadedy/tap/double-shot

"Hey, let's attack the castle!" (voice command while riding a dragon). Ok, you got me there. If that kind of simulation is possible, I want to try it.

Genie 4 is out, Google's first world model for real-time interactive simulation.

I've been following world models for a while. Below are a few interesting points for folks not familiar with world models.

What are world models?
🧠 AI that learns to predict what happens next, then uses that to plan and learn
🔮 LLMs predict the next word, world models predict what happens next in the world
🏗️ Main approaches: JEPA (LeCun), Genie 4 (DeepMind), Marble (World Labs), Cosmos (NVIDIA)
🆕 Genie 4 (announced today) simulates interactive 3D worlds frame by frame, in real time, with native audio

Use cases of world models:
🤖 Robotics: plan motions, train on imagined trajectories (DeepMind paired Genie 4 with Gemini in robotics research)
🚗 Driving: Waymo built its World Model on Genie 3 to simulate edge cases
🎮 Games and VR: steer live worlds with text, like changing weather or adding characters
🎬 Creative industries: filmmaking, journalism, gaming, manufacturing
📊 Enterprise “what-if” simulation before acting

Advantages of world models:
💰 Cheaper and safer than physical testing
📉 Synthetic data where real data is slow and expensive
🧩 Better causal reasoning and long-horizon planning than LLMs
🔊 Richer simulations: Genie 4 adds audio, dialogue and more realistic physics
🤝 Pairs with LLMs: Genie 4 uses Gemini models to keep scenes coherent

Some caveats:
⏱️ Genie 4 stays consistent for only about two minutes, and details drift over longer runs
🔒 Genie 4 is research preview only, for trusted testers
📏 A May 2026 benchmark found no model above 52% on physical consistency
🔥 Resource-hungry, and they can still hallucinate

Future of world models:
💸 Over $3B in VC went to world-model startups in H1 2026
🚀 DeepMind calls world simulation a crucial step toward AGI
🔀 Likely a hybrid future: LLMs, agents and world models combined
🧪 Wider Genie 4 access is coming soon via Project Genie and the Gemini API
🎯 Evaluation needs to go beyond visual realism
